items.title: Natural Law has primary precepts and secondary rules
items.claim: What are Aquinas's primary precepts of natural law?

options.text: Five primary precepts identified by Aquinas: preservation of life, reproduction, education of offspring, living in society, worship of God — secondary precepts (specific moral rules) are derived by reason
Only one rule — do good and avoid evil

items.reveal:
Aquinas's natural law theory appears in the Summa Theologiae I-II (Questions 90-97). The eternal law is God's plan; natural law is rational creatures' participation in it; human law derives specific rules.

The doctrine of double effect — an action with a foreseen bad consequence can be permissible if the bad effect is not intended, the act itself is not intrinsically wrong, and the good outweighs the bad — is a key application (used in modern bioethics, especially end-of-life care).

Natural law is the basis of Catholic moral teaching on contraception, abortion and end-of-life care. John Finnis and Germain Grisez developed 'New Natural Law' (from 1980).
items.why: Catholic ethics is not arbitrary doctrine — it rests on a developed rational framework. Engaging with natural law requires understanding the structure (primary, secondary, double effect) rather than treating it as a list of forbidden actions.

items.title: British religious affiliation has dropped sharply since the 1960s
items.claim: What does the 2021 UK Census show about religion?

options.text: For the first time, less than half of England and Wales (46.2%) identified as Christian; 37.2% had no religion; Islam grew to 6.5%; Hindu, Sikh, Jewish, Buddhist and Other religions made up the remainder
All religions are at the same percentage

items.reveal:
The 2001 Census recorded 72% Christian; 2011 recorded 59%; 2021 recorded 46% in England and Wales. The 'no religion' category rose from 15% (2001) to 25% (2011) to 37% (2021). Scotland (2022 census) showed similar trends; Northern Ireland remains more religious.

Muslim population: 3% (2001), 5% (2011), 6.5% (2021).

Secularisation theory (Bryan Wilson, Peter Berger) predicted declining religious influence with modernity. The reality has been more complex — declining institutional affiliation alongside persistent or growing 'spiritual but not religious' identification and increasing pluralism.
items.why: British religion is restructured, not just declining. The Census numbers show a more religiously plural country where institutional Christianity has lost its majority position — major implications for education, ethics and public life.

items.title: William James identified four marks of mystical experience
items.claim: What are James's four marks of mystical experience?

options.text: Ineffability (cannot be fully described), noetic quality (provides knowledge), transiency (does not last long), passivity (the subject feels acted upon) — set out in 'The Varieties of Religious Experience' (1902)

items.reveal:
James's Gifford Lectures (1901-02) became 'The Varieties of Religious Experience'. He aimed to study religion empirically as a phenomenon of consciousness, regardless of any metaphysical truth claims.

His four marks were intended as descriptive criteria, not arguments for divine reality. Richard Swinburne ('The Existence of God', 1979) and others later used religious experience evidentially — the principle of credulity (we should believe perceptions unless we have reason not to) and the principle of testimony.

Critics including Walter Kaufmann and Steven Katz have argued that mystical experience is heavily shaped by prior cultural framework — a Buddhist's experience is structured by Buddhist concepts.
items.why: Religious experience is studied both descriptively (what do people report?) and evaluatively (what does it prove?). James's framework remains the starting point for both — a century of subsequent debate has built on his typology.
